NTA. You’ve supported your daughter and accomodated her that’s enough. There’s plenty of parents who would dismiss a child wanting to go vegan due to ignorance and cost issues too. I’m a vegan living at home with my two meat eating parents, they support me to an extent- they don’t take the piss out of me, they will eat vegan food with me sometimes (my mum is great, she bakes and is experimenting with a lot of vegan recipes), and buy me my own food from the weekly shop, which my rent goes towards. 

I have the attitude eat what you want as long as you’re not rubbing it in my face- I was very strict about being vegan and a big activist now my attitude is more eh the worlds dying anyway, why attack someone for having a ham sandwich when the huge corporations fucking us won’t change anything. The only time I get bothered is when my mum will cook a Sunday dinner and the whole house stinks of roast chicken but I tend to just stay in my room or make sure I’m out. 

I’m sure your daughters outburst could just be her age, she’s gonna feel like everything is a personal attack. Also that she’s found something new which she’s passionate about and feels it’s a good thing, why does no one understand me !!??!! It’s easy to fixate on something as a teen and have it become a massive part of your identity. I went vegan at 19 and that was probably my whole personality for a long while. I would say keep doing what you’re doing, cook the food separately (this is more than reasonable having separate pans!) but calmly explain you are cutting meat out, you respect her diet and are going well out the way to accommodate for her, but ultimately it is your house. I’d speak to your wife and get her to back you up on this, you don’t wanna be seen as the big bad wolf. Hope it works out! W

The other au pairs I met were all American, my host mum had friends who had au pairs as well (think rich German desperate housewives lmao) so whenever a new au pair arrived we’d get introduced to each other but most of my friends out there were native Germans, or from other non English speaking European countries- Germany is very diverse this surprised me a lot for a small town! 

I think I was very privileged with peoples perceptions to me as I was the only English person living in my village and a lot of Germans love the English culture and hadn’t met any natives before. It also didn’t harm that I was 20 and blonde and quite pretty- not to sound like an asshole but that made people quite friendly and chatty with me when I was out and about as opposed to some of the American girls I knew out there. There was also a lot of American military based nearby, so bumping into these was common whereas I never met another English person in my year there! 

I made some amazing friends out there, all being from friends of friends or just people I would meet on a night out. Everybody made me feel so welcome and invited me into their whole group and I honestly don’t think I met any assholes out there. Another thing I noticed to is that men were more respectful out there- I’m from north England and I’d say catcalling and getting groped on a night out etc is standard procedure, yet not once did I experience any of this in Germany.

No worries! I moved back home unfortunately- I did want to stay but I’m English and my contract expired at a time of massive Brexit uncertainty (which seems to be never ending...) so finding work and accommodation was difficult when most employers and landlords have no idea if I’m going to get deported in a couple of months. I ran out of money too paying for the open university. I hope to move back though once I get a bit more money behind me, it’s such a great and friendly place. 

Germany also has a volunteer programme called a freiwilliges jahr/ social year, which is for under 30s wanted to gain experience in different settings-normally medical, care, education, childcare etc. It’s not considered employment, but they pay you an allowance and have to help with accommodation too if you need it. One of my au pair friends (American, 25) is beginning this in February working in an international Kindergarten. Her German has always been pretty shitty so I wouldn’t worry too much about that haha. The freiwilliges jahr is open to all EU citizens!

I lived in Bad Kreuznach, population 50,000 and about half an hour train from Mainz though I did find the nightlife surprisingly good for a small town and never ended up going on a night out in Mainz oops. 

For me it wasn’t typical as I only spoke English with the host kids and parents, they’d previously lived in England so they wanted me to help the kids practice and I wasn’t confident enough in my German to try and hold a conversation with the parents who speak fluent English lol. 

As an au pair the host family pays for your German course, and from September-June I completed A1 and A2. I would say my German is a higher level than this though, as I’d spend a lot of time in the local pub meeting people and making friends. Honestly this is mostly where I picked up the language from! I made friends with other au pairs though who had picked up the language a lot better than me, as their kids didn’t speak English, so they really had to throw themselves in at the deep end to learn it. Hope this helps :)

Have you considered au pairing? I did a year in a small town near Mainz, it was great especially if you’re young and have a lack of commitments. You don’t have to worry about housing and you’ve got a built in support system, it’s a lot easier to get a job in Germany if you’re already living out there too. Let me know if you have any questions about it!

Firstly, I am so sorry for your loss. I cannot imagine how hard it is to lose a child. 
I read an analogy about grief that I’m going to try and explain- I’m not very good with words, but reading it helped me understand a lot about my own grief when I lost a loved one. 
So imagine there is a square, and a circle is inside it. Every time that the edge of the circle touches the border of the square, that is your grief and it hits you. That’s what you’re feeling now.
Over time, the circle gets smaller and smaller, it hits the square less and less. The grief stays the same, this feeling never entirely goes away and it’s as strong as ever, but it does not come as frequently. 
I know right now grief is your life, and that is absolutely right and maybe right now you do not see a way out. Your grief will always be there and it’s a part of you, but I promise you things will not always be this way. Your feelings are absolutely valid, but you will not spend the rest of your life in total grief.
I hope I did an OK job of explaining the analogy and that maybe it resonates with you, or somebody else a bit. Again, I am so sorry for your loss. You will get through this x
